analysis.one_liner: Requires public companies to disclose climate risks and greenhouse gas emissions to investors.
analysis.headline: Sen. Warren introduced the bill in September 2018 with 8 Democratic cosponsors, but it never received a hearing or vote and died in the Senate Banking Committee when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Securities and Exchange Commission to require every publicly traded company to disclose, in its annual report, its greenhouse gas emissions, the fossil fuel assets it owns or manages, and how it plans to manage climate-related risks. Companies would have to run their numbers under a scenario where the world limits warming to 2 degrees Celsius, which would show how much of a fossil fuel company's value could vanish if the world moves off oil, gas, and coal. The goal was to give savers and investors an honest picture of climate risk and steer money away from assets that could become worthless.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary savers and investors, including anyone with a 401(k) or pension invested in the stock market, would get standardized, comparable information about how climate change and the shift to clean energy could hurt the companies they own. The broader public would also gain: the SEC would have to post the companies' emissions and fossil fuel asset data on its website, creating a public accounting of who is holding what.

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires the SEC to write rules making every public company disclose its direct and indirect greenhouse gas emissions and the share of its assets tied to fossil fuels.

Companies would have to analyze their finances under both a baseline scenario of runaway warming and a scenario where global warming is kept to 2 degrees or lower, exposing how much fossil fuel-related value could become stranded.
Companies that develop oil, gas, or coal would have to detail emissions from combustion, leaks, and land use, plus their methane leak detection methods and freshwater withdrawals.

The SEC would make the disclosed data publicly available on its website in an interactive format, and the Government Accountability Office would periodically audit how well the SEC enforces the rules.
The bill expresses the sense of Congress that standardized climate disclosure will increase transparency about risk accumulation in financial markets and guide capital toward a low-emissions economy.

analysis.who_pays: Publicly traded companies, especially oil, gas, and coal producers, would bear the cost of measuring, verifying, and reporting emissions and climate risk every year. Fossil fuel producers face the larger, deliberate cost: honest accounting under a 2-degree scenario could force a write-down of reserves they currently book as assets, cutting their market value and raising their cost of capital.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and all public companies

drawbacks.text: Compliance is real work: the bill requires audited-style emissions accounting, scenario analysis over at least 30-year time frames, and interactive data tagging, which would burden every public company, not just oil and gas producers.

The bill hard-codes a government-set minimum 'social cost of carbon' price that every company must use in its financial analyses, which critics would call embedding a policy judgment into financial reporting rather than leaving pricing to markets.
Disclosure alone does not cut a single ton of emissions; companies might produce lengthy boilerplate reports that satisfy the letter of the law without changing behavior.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core of the bill is information, not prohibition: companies would have to tell the truth about climate risk, and investors could price it. The honest costs are the reporting burden on public companies and the risk that fossil fuel reserve values get repriced, which is partly the point. The weakest part is the mandated minimum carbon price, which goes beyond disclosure into dictating analytical assumptions. On balance, the transparency benefits to savers outweigh the compliance costs, though the bill would not by itself reduce emissions.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which never held a hearing or markup on it, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the Climate Risk Disclosure Act of 2018 on September 24, 2018, joined by seven Democratic colleagues: Sens. Whitehouse, Schatz, Markey, Booker, Merkley, Harris, and Gillibrand.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
No further action appears in the record: the bill never received a hearing, a committee markup, or a floor vote, and died at the end of the 115th Congress on January 3, 2019.
Had it advanced, the bill would have required SEC rules within one year forcing public companies to disclose emissions, fossil fuel assets, and climate risk strategies in annual reports.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Publicly traded companies, above all oil, gas, and coal producers, came out ahead: they never had to measure and publish their emissions or test their balance sheets against a low-carbon future, so reserve valuations and current business practices went unexamined. Investors and retirement savers went without the standardized climate risk data the bill promised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers and public companies

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.role: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited seven Democratic cosponsors on the day of introduction.

for.name: Sens. Whitehouse, Schatz, Markey, Booker, Merkley, Harris, and Gillibrand
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, making all eight Senate supporters Democrats.

against.name: Sen. Mike Crapo
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, took no action on the bill after referral; no hearing or markup appears in the record, and the bill died in committee.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so positions were never tested on the floor, but all eight Senate supporters were Democrats and the bill sat untouched in a committee led by a Republican chair with a Republican Senate majority.

industries.note: The bill would have forced them to disclose emissions from every barrel and lump of coal, describe how their reserves fare under a 2-degree warming limit, and reveal methane leak and water practices. That accounting could have forced write-downs of reserves they currently book as assets, threatening their market value. Their interest in keeping that information off the books runs against investors' and the public's interest in seeing it.

industries.industry: Publicly traded companies across all sectors
industries.note: Every issuer filing annual reports would have faced new emissions measurement, scenario analysis, and interactive data tagging requirements. Financial, insurance, transportation, electric power, and energy firms were singled out for industry-specific metrics. The burden is real, but the disclosure also protects the companies' own shareholders.

Standardized, comparable climate risk data would let fund managers and retirement savers see which holdings are exposed to physical and transition risks, and the SEC would post the data publicly. Better information directly serves people whose savings are in the market.
